vignette:
She is 63 now, a financial analyst whose days are organized around spreadsheets, forecasts, and the quiet reassurance of numbers that add up. In the office, colleagues know her as precise and composed. She arrives early, keeps her desk immaculate, and rarely speaks about her life outside work. What they do not see is how much of this order has been built against an earlier life that was shattered by chaos.

She grows up in an African country that becomes increasingly dangerous around her. At first, the changes are gradual enough to deny. There are rumors, then disappearances, then armed men in places where children used to play. She remembers learning to read her mother’s face before she learned to read the news. Adults stop speaking freely, lowering their voices when names are mentioned. At night she lies awake, listening for engines, boots, shouting. She begins to understand that safety is something that can vanish while the furniture in the room stays exactly the same.

The event she returns to most often happens when she is still a young woman. Violence comes close to home with terrifying speed. There is gunfire, screaming, people running in every direction. She sees bodies in the street and the stunned, vacant look on faces she has known all her life. In the rush to flee, there is no real decision, only movement. She leaves with almost nothing, separated from people she loves, not knowing who will survive or whether she will ever come back. The journey out is marked by hunger, uncertainty, and the constant need to stay alert. Even after crossing a border and reaching relative safety, her body does not believe it. She sleeps lightly, if at all, waking at the smallest sound, convinced someone is entering.

Refugee life teaches her to expect instability. She waits in lines, fills out forms, depends on strangers’ decisions. She learns quickly that telling her story can be necessary and unbearable at the same time. Every interview requires her to reopen what she is trying desperately to seal shut. She notices that parts of her memory feel seared into her mind—the crack of gunfire, the smell of sweat and dust, the sight of people trampling one another in panic—while other parts are blank. She is ashamed of what she cannot remember and even more ashamed that she survived when others did not.

When she eventually resettles, she commits herself to building a life that cannot be easily taken away. She studies, works hard, and enters finance, where discipline is rewarded and emotions can be kept at a distance. Numbers become a refuge. If she can reconcile an account, forecast a budget, find an error hidden in thousands of entries, she feels briefly steadied. Yet the same hypervigilance that makes her excellent at work follows her everywhere. In meetings, she tracks every movement in the room, noting who enters late, who raises their voice, where the exits are. If someone drops a stack of files or slams a door, her heart races so suddenly that she has to grip the table to keep from jolting visibly.

Over the years, she becomes increasingly alone. She is single and says this matter-of-factly, but it gradually becomes clear how much intimacy has come to feel dangerous. She does not like being asked personal questions. She avoids reunions, community gatherings, and news from her home country because any reminder can pull her back without warning. Sometimes, while reviewing financial reports, a certain phrase, accent, or headline is enough to split the day open. For a few seconds she is no longer in an office; she is running again, unable to find the people she loves. Afterward she feels disoriented and embarrassed, then angry with herself for “still being like this.”

Sleep remains one of her hardest battles. She dreads nighttime because dreams bring back scenes she cannot control. In them, she is searching through crowds, calling names, trying to gather documents that keep slipping from her hands while danger closes in. She often wakes soaked in sweat, her chest tight, already braced for attack. On those mornings she goes to work anyway, exhausted, relying on routine and coffee and the force of habit. She tells almost no one. To others, she appears stoic; inside, she feels as if her nerves are always stretched too thin.

She also carries a persistent sense of foreshortened life, as though some essential part of her future ended when she fled. Even now, decades later, she has trouble making plans that extend too far ahead. She saves money carefully, keeps duplicate copies of important documents, and scans every new environment for risk. She knows these habits helped her survive. She also knows they have narrowed her life. When she speaks about the past, she does so with long pauses, her voice controlled but her hands clenched tightly in her lap, as if the story is still happening somewhere inside her and she must hold herself together while telling it.
